utterances.text: At the end of the statement you will see it is numbered 200, is that a signature of yours? Perhaps you would like to look at the very last page that is stamped page 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is your signature, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What do you mean it is not your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see when I came out of the camp I live in a town where there are very few people from Yugoslavia, and the doctor advised me to talk about the whole incident otherwise I would go crazy, and I said, "I have no one to talk to" and he said, "Well, then take a pen and write it down". So I wrote it down but it was not a statement. I just wrote it as if to have some something to remember as a memento, but I could write this down on 200 pages had I written it as a statement, every detail in all the incidents. But this does not cover all the incidents, everything that I went through while in the camp. This is only a part of it. This is the smallest, the tiniest part of the truth that I experienced in the camps, and that I wish to survive so as not to forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look then at what you said was the truth, because on page 166, if you turn over the first page, you, in fact, wrote in your hand there that it was the truth, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would read that out what it means in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the truth for me all. That I wrote down here is the truth but, of course, you can twist words as you like. A word can be -- one word can be interpreted in a thousand ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But these are your words on these pages, they are not my words, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are my words ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which have a meaning for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps then if you would just turn to page 178 and see what that meaning was concerning Duca. To be fair to you, so that the whole thing is put in full context, can you see that the paragraph that begins, is it ,"Oko 22", the first paragraph on the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you would just read out that whole paragraph so that we can see what you said there? Read it out in your own language, then it will be translated back to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Around 2200 a new group of torturers came again, and they were preparing torture for us. As there was no electricity, they would put the generator in the corridor and a lamp bulb so that they could light the corridor and the small room which was the torture room for them. "They took the list which dammed Krkan had compiled and called out one by one and tortured him. That group of Chetniks was composed of six which included Dule Tadic from Kozarac, Simo Kevic from Orlovci, a tyre repairer, one Banovic from Prijedor, Dule called 'Duca' from Prijedor and Dragan Babic from Babici near Kamicani. "Amid the guards were the guards Krkan and two brothers, Kvocka. The moment they would called out one, a noose would be thrown around his neck so that he could not shout, whereas others would start beating with different objects, rods made of some flexible" -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all we need at this stage so that the full text concerning the names was read out. You see, I was interested in you saying in here that Duca was also called Dule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some people called him that in Keraterm. I knew him as "Duca" and most people knew him as "Duca".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but why were you trying to avoid admitting that to us in this courtroom, that you knew him as "Dule" and saying it was a mistake or saying it was not intended? Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not want to avoid it and I am not avoiding it now. To my mind, it is the same, "Dule" and "Duca".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: OK. How long was it then that this group of men attacked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not attack. It was I already described it. They brought me. I greeted them. They tightened the noose around my neck and beat me up. How long it took, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That seems to have been your fourth beating that you had had since arriving at the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first real beating. The other thing was beating along the way, on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By this stage you must have been in a very poor physical condition, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would not say very poor, but I was in a poor condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, again when you were called out you knew what was in store for you, you were in great fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I did not know what was in store for me, but I heard beatings and I saw all those people thrown out. So that I could assume that the same thing was in store for me as for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Later on after your beating you have told us about an occasion when you say Dule Tadic came into your room and said, "You will remember, Sivac, that you cannot touch a Serb or say anything to a Serb", is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not come to my room. He stayed in the doorway when they threw in in front of my feet Sefik Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that you recognised that first person as being Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that because you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that what you were telling us about earlier today, that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, in this statement here you actually say that you identified Dule Tadic by his voice. If you turn to the next page, page 179 ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also heard him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps so that you can have an opportunity to deal with this, you can read out the last paragraph that begins, is it "Nekako" or "Nekako", the last paragraph on page 179?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can just read out that bit that is on the page, the full paragraph in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last one you mean, from "Hrvat" or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A few lines above there right at the beginning so that we have the whole paragraph. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. "It could have been the third night, around the midnight, I was awake once again and thirsty. A guy gave me a few drops of water and I was refreshed. Outside the Chetniks indulged in orgies and I heard them calling out again somebody called Hrvat. That night they killed him and then they threw in an industrious lad who asked for water but had no time to drink it because he died. I heard the one throwing him in swear, and I recognised Dule Tadic's voice because he swore this in the same way that night when they beat me. In the morning I saw that the killed man was Sefik Sivac. All around there were dead who were being taken out by other prisoners".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, when you wrote about this you did not say that you saw Dule Tadic at all, did you? You said that you recognised the voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard a voice before while he was swearing and I saw him the moment when he was throwing Sefik at my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What you heard being said was those words about "You will remember, Sivac, that you cannot touch a Serb or saying anything to a Serb". That is what you were talking about hearing, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, "You will remember, Sivac, that you may not say a word to a Serb or lay a finger on a Serb", something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this statement here that you have just read out to us, you say that it was in the morning that you knew the killed man was Sefik Sivac? You described him earlier as an industrious young man; what your words were, "In the morning I saw that the killed man was Sefik Sivac".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised him in the morning and then I was positive that it was he. At the moment when they threw him in, I was not sure that that was he, but he was not industrious, he was a worthy man, a big man. An industrious man is a man who works a lot and things like that, and the word I meant was that he was a very big man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So there was some doubt in your mind that caused you not to be able to recognise the man when he was put in the room, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment that is quite correct, I did not recognise him at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that because the room was in darkness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could also be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that because it was difficult for you to recognise someone in that room with no electricity at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no light in that room at night, and it really was difficult to see the face of a beaten man. But when the day broke there was enough light to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say about this lighting equipment that was brought into the white house that night that you were beaten, is that true? Did that really happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did happen and I shall never forget it. I will not forget my broken ribs and pain and the painful bones that I still suffer from today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand that. What I am asking you about, however, is the lighting because in this statement that we have been looking at you say that the lighting was run by a generator, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not a dynamo generator. It was the one that was used in a car or dry batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the lighting was poor, was it, unless you had some sort of artificial light to enable you to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was enough to light the corridor, and they also lit that small room. Now, whether there were two lamp bulbs there in the small room, I did not see that, but at any rate they were well lit, both the corridor and the small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it is not a generator that was being used to power the light, it was a car battery, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and that was a car battery or a truck battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to these matters, you have given many interviews to the press and media? Have you been on television about these matters, Mr. Icic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not on television. This incident was not discussed. The television was interested in what men worth 100 francs looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but you have spoken to, is it, Monika Gras? Have you been on one of her television programmes or a couple of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have given interviews to journalists, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, what I am suggesting to you is that you did not recognise Dusko Tadic in the white house on these occasions that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the right to say that I had not been to the white house, but I claim that he was in these two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw the arrest of Dusko Tadic on television, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the arrest itself because I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but you watched it on television when you got home from work that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only briefly during the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have also watched programmes about Omarska that have been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not much, very little. I had no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you have spoken to television journalists; Penny Marshall is another one you have spoken to, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Marshal came to see me not long ago, but we had never mentioned Tadic or even the incident. She asked me if I was going to The Hague and we just chatted. She came to my company, she came to see where I worked, and we did not discuss this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know who I mean by witness K in this case? I do not want the person's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness K, yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is she your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, before the witness answers, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Wait. Do not answer. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with witness K. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can appreciate, your Honours, there has been a change.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one minute. OK. The witness has changed since I took my earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The status of the witness has changed, K, which I was advised of this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We informed the Defence this morning that as of yesterday witness K had indicated her willingness and her wish to testify publicly. We will be providing her name and the statement without redactions to the Defence today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. You have not advised the Court or have you?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have entered an order on August 10th, I guess, of last year granting the protective measures that the Prosecutor had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, fine. If it is fine with the parties, let us discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not know the name yet which is why I am still using the initial. [To the witness]: But is it right that she is your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, I think we are entering into ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she is not my brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am just a little confused about where we are now as I imagined we would have to be in the light of the answers. I understood that we may or may not be talking about the same person when K is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: From what Miss Hollis tells me, the K that was referred to in the order of August 10th 1995 now wishes to testify openly and freely. So, if that is the wish of the party who intends on offering that witness, then that may be done. So at this point I have no questions. It is up to Mr. Kay, I suppose, to elicit from the witness what he wishes. If there is no objection, then we can go ahead. My only concern was that a witness who was the subject of protective measures, a request made by the Prosecutor, would be identified and then unbeknown to the Chamber, at least, that request has been withdrawn. That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will leave this area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No further questions. You may go into the area, Mr. Kay, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have made claims that 30 to 40 people were being killed in the white house each night that you were there, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there was more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there more people were killed. They were carried away. Whether they were dead, they were really killed, they never came back, none of them or none of the ones who were carried away from the white house. That is why I assumed they are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But that would have been almost your entire room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost the whole room emptied out, almost the whole room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Icic, you were asked whether or not you knew why you were included among the group of people taken from Keraterm to Omarska. You indicated that, to this day, you really do not know why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated in Omarska, did the person questioning you note in your statement that you had been a worker in Germany, that you had come home to visit and then had been unable to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was his reaction when he saw that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he smiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have this photograph marked as the exhibit next in order for identification, please. It will be Exhibit 279. Mr. Usher, may that be shown to the Defence, please. Mr. Icic, do you recognise that photograph as showing a portion of the white house and, in particular, showing a portion of the small room at the end of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except those things, the tables, it was not there. It was all empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender 279 for admission, your Honour, and ask that it be placed on the Elmo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 279 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we focus in a little more closely toward that rear room? Perhaps a little farther back. Mr. Icic, the room at the back end of the corridor is the beating room you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can see the left wall and the rear wall in that photograph, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does the rear wall extend farther to the right and then is there another wall on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there off to the right and then there is another wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that room the size of a shower cubicle, at least shower cubicles in your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you would rather say the size of a bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is there room in that -- is there space in that room for six people to be inside and to move about, at least to move their arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that room there was space for me to fall down and for them to beat me. How they behaved there, how they moved, I did not see that and how they arranged it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Icic, referring to other parts of the white house, you indicated that you did not observe either that there were not doors or you did not observe doors on the second room to the left, the second room to the right in that small room we just discussed. Do you recall whether or not there were doors on the first rooms to the left and right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a closed door on the first room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that the same type of door that we have seen in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, half glass door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify one or actually two incidents that Mr. Kay asked you about a few moments ago. When you had returned from interrogation and a group of people came in and were jumping on your backs and cutting your clothes ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Krkan was there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krkan was in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that was over and sometime later did Krkan return with the paper and pencil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only after some time, he came with paper and a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about a person that you had seen in Keraterm known as Duca. You did not know Duca's real first name or last name, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I do not know it now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that Duca could be a nickname for a number of first names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I also want to ask you about one other incident that Mr. Kay referred to, and that was the occasion when Sefik Sivac was thrown into your room. First of all, before Mr. Sivac was thrown into the room, did you hear something in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard a curse and some kind of quarrel or they were really cursing, they were discussing when they were beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you heard that cursing was Mr. Sivac then thrown into your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that they dragged him in and they threw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was no light in your room. Was the hall ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no light.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the hallway and doorway better illuminated than the interior of your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hallway was lit and it was lit well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the face of the first man who dragged Mr. Sivac to the room and threw him in as he stood at the doorway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that man Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure it was Dule Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it after Mr. Sivac was thrown in that you heard Dule Tadic say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time he said those words that for Sefik to remember that Serbs cannot be touched or be said -- and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So first you heard the cursing, then Mr. Sivac was thrown in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you heard the words about Sivac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Icic, you have told us about the account which you wrote in 1993 about some of the experiences you had in Omarska and Keraterm. Are you a professional writer, Mr. Icic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I never wrote anything and this I wrote only not in order not to go crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you a criminal investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you a historian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you trying to write an account for courtroom purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That would look completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, for example, when you wrote about the incident with Sefik Sivac, did you write each and every detail of what happened that particular night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not write down every detail. It would be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you write down each and every basis for why you knew it was Dule Tadic who threw Mr. Sivac in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not write down. I did not write down why. It was an abbreviated form, so that I have it with me, on me. The reason, I could just assume why they did it, but what I knew I did not have the need to write down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kay asked you if you spoke to journalists such as Monika Gras and you indicated you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He asked you if you saw the arrest of Dusko Tadic or were aware of the arrest of Dusko Tadic, and you indicated that you were aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out from television, from the news when I came back home from work. I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The account you wrote about your experiences or some of your experiences in Omarska and Keraterm, however, was written before Mr. Tadic was arrested, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before you were ever contacted by any journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I was not even thinking about that, that I would get in touch with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was in that account that you recorded that Mr. Tadic and others had beaten you in the small room of the white house and that Mr. Tadic had thrown Sefik Sivac into the room, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question I did not ask you earlier. Mr. Icic, do you see Dule Tadic in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point him out and tell us what he is wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is in a green jacket with a tie between two policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May the record reflect the identification of the accused, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have just a moment. Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, we have seen some photographs of the inside of the white house, and those photographs show nice, clean white walls. Was that the condition of the white house when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time the condition was as if it was a very messy slaughterhouse, stench and blood, urine and beaten up people, blood sprayed on the walls, horror. That was how the rooms in the white house looked in reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have just one question and it relates to the dates about which you testified. What was the date, as best you can recall, you left Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7th or 8th, I am not sure about that. I cannot say the exact date, 7th or 8th July.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you come to Omarska immediately after leaving Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The beating that you have testified about, am I correct that that occurred a few days after you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beatings happened the same night.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Tieger? Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to this witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Icic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you very much for coming. We will stand in recess now for lunch until 2.30. (12.55 p.m.). (Luncheon Adjournment). (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, will you call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Before I call the next witness, referring to the matter we discussed this morning, as I indicated, witness K has indicated to me last evening that it is now her wish that she testify in public with no protective measures in place. For that reason, I request that that portion of the decision in August that relates to providing protective measures for witness K be withdrawn or rescinded. If the Court approves that, then I am prepared at this time to provide the Defence with the name of the witness, confirming the name of the witness, and also with a statement without the prior redactions that we had.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Do I need to hear from the Defence on that? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection whatsoever, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Yes, Miss Hollis, that request will be granted and that portion of decision granting protective measures to K at the request of the Prosecutor will be modified, at least, or withdrawn, treated appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I appreciate your advising the Chamber. In that way we do not have to be concerned about that matter. Of course, the Chamber is delighted that the witness will come forward and we will hear from the witness in open court.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, it appeared this morning that we were being somewhat dilatory in advising the Chamber. I apologise. We simply were not aware it might come up in cross-examination and we wanted to have the completed package before we notified you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, witness 52 in the order you have will not be called at this time, instead witness 54 will be called. So, your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would call Ermin Strikovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has the Defence been advised of the change in order?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. ERMIN STRIKOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Strikovic, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ermin Strikovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15th July 1957.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What part of Bosnia is Zenica located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the central part.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if we could retrieve Prosecution Exhibit 78, please? If that could be provided to the witness, please? Sir, if would look at that and then if that could be placed on the overhead projector? If we could zoom in on the central part, please? Sir, would you point to where Zenica is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Sir, did you live in Zenica until you were 13 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, until my 13th.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Until your 13th birthday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then did you move to the Puharska area of the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1985 did you move to the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you live in Kozarac until May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA from 1984 until 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a truck driver.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not serve my military in Bosnia. I was in Kovin near Belgrade for training and after that I was posted to Kerestinec near Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During your service in the JNA did you become familiar with JNA uniforms, weapons, vehicles and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what is your marital status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Married.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your wife's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Azra Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her prior occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Veterinary doctor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your prior occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A traffic engineer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a company called iron ore mines Ljubija, truck and vehicle maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the Ljubija iron ore mine also own the mines in Tomasica and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you know, what is the distance from Prijedor to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 22 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would be the average driving time from Prijedor to Omarska under normal conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 45 minutes by bus, passenger car 30, 35 minutes, depending on the traffic conditions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the distance from Kozarac to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would be the normal driving time under normal conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under normal conditions, about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties at the Ljubija iron ore mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the technical manager of the car park of the part of the company called Autoservis.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you work at that company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nine years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was your place of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters were in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were most of your business and social friends and acquaintances located in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know many of the people who lived in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know many people in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In March 1992, do you recall being told to set up a plan to bring iron ore from the Omarska mine to the Tomasica mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember a plan was to be drawn for the reconstruction of the already existing road, industrial access road, between Omarska and Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who ordered you to draw up this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My superior, Bozo Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his position in the company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the manager of that part of the company.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that the plan involved reopening an industrial access road between Tomasica and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The plan would call for what type of vehicles to use that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to be used for heavy duty mining mechanization used to transport iron ore.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that project was underway, did other high level persons consult with you about the progress of the project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were they interested in when the project would be finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who were these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ostoja Marjanovic, general manager of the company, Stevan Tubin, principal co-ordinator, traffic co-ordinator -- company traffic co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The three men that you mentioned in relation to this plan, Mr. Grbic, Mr. Marjanovic and Mr. Tubin, what was the ethnic group of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any of these three men hold high office in any political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ostoja Marjanovic was one of the leaders of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were told that this road would be used for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To transport the iron ore between Omarska and Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that road opened in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if I could offer to the Court another map, Prosecution Exhibit 280, for identification? This map is similar to Prosecution Exhibit 79, but it shows an area further south and it is a different series. We do have a copy for the Defence and we will provide three copies for the Judges. Sir, if you could take a moment to look at that map and orient yourself as to the location of that industrial road you were discussing? Then if Prosecution Exhibit 78 could be removed from the overhead projector and Prosecution Exhibit 280 for identification placed on the projector, please? Sir, if you could show us where that road ran that was reopened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the map].

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could put the pointer on that and hold it on there while we locate it on the cameras? Then if you could show you us the route that that road took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the map].

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that road following beside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 280?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 280 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that road had been opened, did you have an opportunity to examine that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the time you examined it, did you find any evidence that that road was being used by heavy vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not -- this road surface did not look as if any heavy duty vehicles had used it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you later learn what that road was being used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you learn? What was it being used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To transport people to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a considerable number of people, I was also transported along that road to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, several days before the attack on Kozarac, did you become aware of a blockade of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 26th May, do you recall being at the motel in Kozarac that was being used as a temporary medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall surrender terms being agreed upon at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember some of the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you part of the column that surrendered on 26th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the driver of the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was at the head of that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a private passenger car, a Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who were the passengers in that car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac police.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then you followed after that car in your ambulance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you drive your ambulance from Kozarac to the hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Along the way what happened with the car with the police officers in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The column was stopped on the Kozarac/Prijedor road next to a bus stop we used to call Limenka. One of the officers of the army waiting there let through the car that I was driving and another car behind me, and the Mercedes with Kozarac police was stopped at that bus stop.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was that bus stop from the main business area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the commercial centre in Kozarac, about a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you had reached the Prijedor hospital with the ambulance, were you then taken to the Prijedor police station and then on to Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then on the next night, 27th May, were you taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many buses of detainees were taken on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you the accurate number. I could not count them but there were quite a number of them, about 10.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska camp and got off the buses, did you and the others have to go through a line of men in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had to.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw blue camouflage uniforms. I saw dark blue uniforms. They wore berets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These blue camouflage uniforms and dark blue uniforms, were these uniforms you had ever seen before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have never seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you went through the line, did you hear any of the men wearing those uniforms speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard them speaking.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you heard them speaking, were they speaking a local dialect or a non-local dialect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They spoke some other dialect.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the dialect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you able to recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina one does not use the ekavski dialect. It is characteristic only of the territories of Serbia and Montenegro, and that was the dialect that they spoke, the ekavski dialect.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was being done to you and the other detainees as you went through this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were swearing, using filthy language, insulting us, swearing, saying, "Why did you surrender? Why did you not fight, but it is easier this way, it will be easier to kill you this way", and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were any of the detainees being beaten as you went through the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 72 days.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The first night that you were in the camp, do you recall an incident involving a man named Ahil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Ahil from before the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he worked for the police in Kozarac on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to him during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with me in the room that they put us when we arrived in Omarska, and I guess that he was afraid or, perhaps, physically unstable. He starting shouting, "This is never going to be Serbia, this is Bosnia". He said or, rather, he shouted, "This is Bosnia", and at that moment the room was entered by a man dressed in a uniform. I knew him from before -- we used to call him "Cigo" -- and he began to beat Ahil and ended by dealing him a blow with the automatic rifle or, more precisely, with the rifle butt which hit Ahil's head.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did he beat Ahil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahil fell down, and he was lying quite still on the ground and Cigo left the room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did Cigo come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little later Cigo returned and dragged Ahil's body into the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see Ahil again the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was lying on the grass next to the white house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was Ahil's ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahil was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, what was Cigo's ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were at Omarska camp, did it appear to you that Cigo was a camp guard or was a visitor to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cigo was an occasional visitor to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At some point after your arrival at Omarska, were you held in the workshop building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could take that pointer and simply point to and touch the building you referred to as the workshop building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the model].

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were being held in the workshop building, were you held in a room where a man named Vasif Alihodzic was also held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you known him before you came to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. We were friends.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the owner of a small transportation company.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he called out of the room that you were both in at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was called out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you at some point held in a room where a man named Sejad Sivac was also held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you known Sejad Sivac before you came to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were close friends.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his occupation before he was brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a veterinarian.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from the hamlet of Sivci.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was Sejad Sivac taken out for interrogation two times in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was called out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his condition when he returned from his first interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that he returned in a normal shape. He was not beaten up. He looked normal.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his condition when he returned from his second interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the second interrogation he could not enter back into the room by himself. He was carried into the room by others.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any injuries, wounds or bruising on his body at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it because I personally dressed him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Black marks on the back, dark red haemorrhages in the area of the kidneys, again bruises on his legs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long was it before Sejad Sivac could walk again after this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It took five or six days. I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he called out again at some later time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how much later he was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks after the second interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when he was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. That was exactly on July 27th at 1400 hours -- 1420 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How is it that you can remember that so precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time when he was called out he left his personal belongings to me and he stepped out. I knew he was not going to come back and that is why I asked people around me what date it was and what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to him as he left the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. Immediately when he reached the door he got a kick into his chest by the soldier who called him out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see anything after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The doors closed. You could not see anything after that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see your friend again after that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, again the first name of your friend was what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sejad Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you taken to Manjaca from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From August 6th 1992 until December 14 the same year.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you go from Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the collection centre in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Kozarac on 24th May 1992, were you a member of any anti-Serb military or paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you a member of any organised anti-Serb resistance group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the attack on Kozarac on 24th May 1992, did you become a member of any such group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Strikovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are permanently excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time we would call Hakija Elezovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has gone to see if the next witness, I presume, is available because I guess that was a record, Miss Hollis. You should be given an award. I think Mr. Niemann is second after you in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are not trying for awards ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sure you are not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- but we got all the relevant information, I think

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good, thank you. MR. HAKIJA ELEZOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hakija Elezovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: February 1st 1940.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that in the town of Trnopolje or in a hamlet nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was the hamlet of Elezovici.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was the hamlet of Elezovici from Trnopolje town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you live in Elezovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My whole life, up until now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the nationality or ethnic group of the inhabitants of Elezovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Elezovici was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, was the hamlet called Elezovici because it was mostly members of the Elezovic family who lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As for the town of Trnopolje itself, what was the ethnic composition of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mixed. There were different nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was Elezovici from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was it from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your previous occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a fisherman. I was working in the fishing industry.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the ponds of Sanicani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of Sanicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanicani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked from '63 till '92, 29 years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if we could have Prosecution Exhibit 280 put back on the overhead projector, but first hand it to the witness, please? Mr. Elezovic, if you would take a moment to look at that map and find the fish farm where you worked and also where Elezovici was located. Then if that map could be placed on the overhead projector? Sir, if you could show us, first, the fish farm where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. This is the railway station, Kozarac and Trnopolje altogether, and then this is where I lived, here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you hold that for a moment, sir, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, sir. If those maps could be returned to the Registrar? Mr. Elezovic, when the attacks began in opstina Prijedor did you have three children, two sons and one daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the names of your sons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The older was Salih and the younger -----

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the name of your younger son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samir.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your sons' dates of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salih was born in '64, April 27th.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Samir was born when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 73, also in April. I do not quite remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you lived in Elezovici, did you ever travel into the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why would you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an office there, there was a market and then my wife also had her family in Kozarusa and so ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we were to talk about an average, monthly average, how often would you go to Kozarac in a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite say. Sometimes I would not go at all, sometimes five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him from sight, but up until the conflict I did not know him really. I just know him from the sight.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you known him by sight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five or six years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went to Kozarac was he someone you would see frequently, occasionally, or seldom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not every time I went, but I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any of your children know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my older son knew him well. They even were friends.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your older son, Salih, ever talk to you about Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not -- I was not too interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware if Dule Tadic had any kind of businesses in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew he had a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where that cafe was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where would that be located in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a location as you went up the main street on the right-hand side as you walk from the direction towards Mrakovica, up from the school a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what business or businesses were located on the opposite side of the street from his cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the other side of the cafe were -- there was a hair salon, I think there was a pharmacy, as I recall, and a book store or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever go to his cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion only.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you knew Dule Tadic to see him, did you ever see him with a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, at this time I would ask you to look around the courtroom and see if you see Dule Tadic from Kozarac in the courtroom, and if he is, I would ask you to point to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you tell us also where he is seated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left-hand side between the two policemen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask a correct identification of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. The record will reflect that the witness properly identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that at the beginning of the attack on Kozarac you had two sons, Salih and Samir. Had your son Salih been mobilized as a reserve officer when the conflict in Croatia began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did he serve as a reserve officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not even a month and a half, about one month and 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why did he leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why he left, because he saw that it was no war, that it was leading nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, were the non-Serb inhabitants of the Trnopolje area ordered to turn in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To turn in weapons, who had it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a hunting rifle, but it was from, belonged to the company so I returned it. It was not my own so I returned it to the director.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you turn this hunting rifle in before or after the attacks began in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned it before.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your sons have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you and the members of your family at home when Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were all there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did Salih later go to Kamicani to see if his girlfriend and her family were all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was Salih then captured and taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Except for Salih, did you and the rest of your family remain in your home until 9th July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have refugees in your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: From what villages or hamlets had these refugees come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the detention camp that had been opened at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But you were aware that the camp had been opened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How far was this camp from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one kilometre, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your wife and other inhabitants of Trnopolje take food to the detainees at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did this continue until the inhabitants in your area began to be rounded up and taken away as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did the cleansing in the Trnopolje area begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: July 9th, around 5 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was your particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the area up until Rajici and Matici and Elezovici and Trnjani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had the other areas already been cleansed by that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, on 9th July were you and your children helping Serb neighbours in their field before the Serbs soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that day did the soldiers come to your home and force you and your son Samir to join a column that was going down the road toward Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How large a column was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite know, but I believe it was around 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the gender and age groups of the people in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 16 to 70, men.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the men who forced you to leave home and escorted you in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Minja Kecen from Sanicani, there were his colleagues, and then one other person from Zmijanac, but I do not remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said you recognised Mijo Kecen? What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mija Kecen, the son of Bogoljub Kecen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The first name was Minja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Minja, but I think that the real name is Miroslav, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these two men that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the men wearing who forced you from your home and were escorting you in this column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had infantry weapons. They had arms and they had uniforms, different. They had both SMB and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you walking in this column with your son Samir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened as you walked in this column to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the camp, there was a hamlet, Reljici, and first they brought out Esad Mujgic and then my son Samir, Edhem Elezovic and Amir and Halil, the two sons, and then they shot them, about three metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you see them when they shot your son and these other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see who it was who shot your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Minja from Zmijanac and some others that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when your son was taken out from the column, did you have the opportunity to say anything to your son before he was taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was just looking him in the eyes and he was looking back.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to go to your son after he had been shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we moved on another five or six steps and then stopped.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was being done to the other people in the column when these men had been pulled out and shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing -- they were picking out other people, a lot of people were killed there, about 30 at that time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So other people were taken out of the column and killed along the route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Trnopolje camp, were you put on to buses and taken to Omarska camp and then from there sent on to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 days, not longer. I do not know if it was even that long.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
