utterances.text: If I could have Prosecution Exhibit 201 shown on the computer? Sir, what room were you held in at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Room No. 2.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many men were held in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was over 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Keraterm were there people being held in other rooms there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I think there were four rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be handed to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What Exhibit is that, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is Prosecution Exhibit 201. Sir, do you recognise what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. This is a warehouse in Keraterm, the warehouse for tiles, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Keraterm were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did that interrogation take place in a room on the first floor of the Keraterm camp building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the left. You pass by No. 1 and then go upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that photograph could be placed on the overhead projector, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where I went upstairs and here they interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could show us that again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here was a staircase, the stair went up and it is up here where they interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken in for interrogation, who did that interrogation at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radakovic, the Director of the National Park, Kozarac National Park.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic was his bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened during that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they interrogated me, then mostly about my son, and that I was responsible for his leaving the army, for deserting, and they began to beat me. Dule began to -- first he kicked me with his foot and I fell. Then he went around the table and continued to beat me on the back and on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that Dule first kicked you with his foot and you fell? Where did he kick you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the chair. Up here in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he kicked you in the chest, how did he kick you, was it a regular kick or was it a different kind of kick?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That master's kick.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, "a master's kick"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was not -- he did not just kick me, he sort of fooled around then and, I mean, he waited for me to relax a little bit and then he hit me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he kicked you was he facing you straight on or did he kick you from the side with his body to the side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then when I fell down he came round, because he was on the other side of the table, so he went around the table to approach me and continued hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say he was hitting you, what was he hitting you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his feet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he continue to kick you the same way throughout this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one would say that, yes, with his feet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen this kind of kicking before, this kind of kicking and fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen it in films and such like.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of films were these where you saw this kind of kicking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, karate, judo.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, how long did this beating last with Dule Tadic kicking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could be about a couple of minutes, and the interrogation altogether lasted for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Radakovic joining in on this beating of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radakovic was in the room. He interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he also beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. He simply grinned and laughed as this one was beating me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that when they were interrogating you and talking to you, they were talking mostly about your son. That was your son Salih?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Salih.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did they say about your son Salih?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I was responsible, that I advised him to leave the army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they say anything about you meeting your son or being reunited with your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Radakovic said, "Sentenced to death" and he said, "You will have an opportunity to see him in Omarska", that I was going to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this incident when Dule Tadic was beating you, in total throughout this incident, how long did you look at Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see him clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was he wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a police uniform on then.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons on his person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, did he have any facial hair or was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, shorter beard than usually.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer from that beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My ribs were broken.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you suffer any other injuries in addition to your ribs being broken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kidneys, and I have headaches.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty breathing after that interrogation and beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident that occurred in room 3 at Keraterm later that day after Dule Tadic beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in room 3, one could hear noise, fires being shot, intensive fires. I mean, it looked like some substantial weapons, like machine gun or something like that. Many people were killed that day, and that Zigic took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you actually see what was happening or you simply heard things during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could hear it and afterwards I saw blood, several hours later it had not been washed away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who were being held in room 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew three brothers from Rakovcani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say that several hours later you saw blood outside. Was that the next day that you saw blood outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day when I started for Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It was the next day then that you were taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska camp were you and other detainees with you forced to line up against a building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what position did you have to place your hands and fingers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three fingers against the wall like this.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was done to you and the other detainees after you were up against the wall with your hands in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us, all of us, but that building helped me because when he hit me, it was Cigo, and I fell down and I threw up all this coagulated blood and then I could breathe more easily.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say it was Cigo who hit you. Had you known Cigo from before Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know he was born in Omarska and was a taxi driver in Prijedor. I did not know him particularly well but I have known him for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken after this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the white house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what room were you kept in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not a room really. It was a toilet-come-bathroom, but it was not completed. There were two rooms on one side, two on the other and straight ahead was the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this toilet or bathroom you were kept in was at the very end of the hall in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: There were two rooms on the left and two rooms on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were put into that bathroom area, how crowded was that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 30 of us, in a small area, 30 of us. It was packed. We did not have enough air to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to sit down or lie down in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we could not sit down, all of us, nobody could lie down.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that you could not breathe. Were there any windows into that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a small window in the middle of the room, rather high up, and it was closed and we were asking from us money so they could buy beer and then they would open the window for us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was asking you money to buy beer and then they would open the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards, camp guards.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in this small room crowded together like that, did anyone in that room die from the conditions in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know his name. He was rather fat and that must be why he died, and there was another one -- another one also.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that when you first arrived at Omarska camp you were beaten by a man you knew as Cigo. Do you recall another occasion when Cigo beat you in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, another time in the white house he forced me to kneel down and bark like a dog, and then I was barking and he pushed the barrel into my mouth and said, "Oh, you want to bite me, do you?"

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he do to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He broke my teeth down there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your bottom teeth in front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you arrived at Omarska did you on any occasion see your son Salih?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him once queuing for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to talk with him when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the first occasion that you were taken to the building that had the kitchen and you were taken there for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to you when you got to the top of the stairs in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they brought me to the top of the stairs and there was a group of people up there and they immediately started beating me. I had barely lifted my head at the top of the stairs, somebody hit me and kicked out my front, upper front teeth.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they continue to beat you after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they beat me up but I still could walk. They beat me and then they left me, and then I went to the end, to the room at the end, to the left and that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went into that room for interrogation and they asked you questions, were you able to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not right away, and then he said, "Well, talk. Has your tongue been cut out?" but my mouth was full of blood so I simply could not talk for a while.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the kind of questions they were asking you during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the organisation, who was arming it, who had I voted for. They were simply looking for a reason to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that interrogation were you taken back to the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: About an hour later were you called out again for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went up the stairs of that same building for the second interrogation, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then at the top of the stairs there were more army. Radakovic was watching and said, "Oh, you are back to get it" and he hit me and I fell down, and they took me back to the white house and they did not take me for any further interrogation, only up the stairs and then a policeman took me to the white house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Radakovic who was up the stairs, is this the same Radakovic who interrogated you at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken back to the white house, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the white house, upstairs to the right.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken back to the white house, to the white house where you had been held before, were you taken into the white house at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me in for interrogation. When I came back from the interrogation for the second time, they did not take me in. The second time they took me to beat me again.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did they take you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the white house, there was tall grass there. There were some holes, and there were about 10, up to 10, soldiers beating. There was already a heap of dead and that is where I saw my son being beaten. I knew those five or six people who were there. Dule was the first to meet me. He started with his foot and said, "Now you have come to the right place", and began to beat me and my son was crying, "Let my old man go", and then he got after my son, and when I started standing up somebody struck me on the neck and I fell again. I received a very severe blow and then I was unconscious for quite some time. When I came too, and they were already loading the dead, and I must have been unconscious for an hour or two. There were very many dead. There was my son and Sivac, the veterinarian, what is his name, Sivac, I have forgotten his name, but I know he was the veterinarian. They were already lying one on top of the other. Then I recognised Redo and then a football player. They were dead already. They were very many dead there. The truck was full of dead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a man named Zuhdija Turkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Turkanovic, Turkanovic was there too. Yes, I saw him as well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a person named Nedibov Duracak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Nedib's son, that is a football player, and he was lying there dead, Nedibov Duracak.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go back for a moment? You said that they brought you to the white house, an area where there was tall grass. Was that to the side of the white house, behind the white house? Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind the white house, right where that bathroom was, on the side where the bathroom was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you came around to the back of the white house, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them beating people, a group of those, all soldiers, and Dule with them in camouflage, in camouflage clothes, military uniform, he had a baton, and fighting. They were not firing off their rifles. They were simply beating people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you came around the back and saw Dule Tadic and the others beating the people there, did you recognise your son at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then Dule Tadic began to beat you as well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he was beating you, how was he beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the foot in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These feet to the stomach, was this the same sort of kick that he had used in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, yes, they were similar, those kicks. He really knew how to use his feet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this incident when you saw Dule Tadic behind the white house, do you have any idea how long it was you were actually able to look at him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not long, five or six minutes. When my son said to let me go, not to beat me, he left me and then got after my son with a pistol and then my son fell. After that I was struck very badly. There was a severe blow and I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw Dule Tadic on that day, do you recall if he was clean shaven or if he had facial hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His beard was longer than in Keraterm, not really big beard but it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you said that when you regained consciousness they were loading the bodies. When you regained consciousness, who were you lying next to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was lying near my son and Sivac and that Turkanovic, those who were near me, and then I recognised immediately those who were killed before. There were bodies all over the grass. There were very many of them. They loaded a truck full of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were loading the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were those people from the camp, Samir Hodzic, he was the one who took my son and Sivac. There was another one, I know he had bread in Prijedor. He was an Albanian, I believe. He took me, he and this Hodzic took me, to the white house when it was all over and they dumped me in the first room.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw them loading your son, you said Samir Hodzic was loading your son, did you notice what Samir Hodzic was wearing on his feet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was bare foot, and then he took a pair of footwear and put them on.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Whose footwear did he take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son's, Salih's.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After he took that footwear, did he say anything to you about wearing your son's shoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I told him to take them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So then after this, after you regained consciousness, you were taken back into the white house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they took us in there. The guards did not even notice. There was a guard who paid no attention. He was sitting up there. There was, to the left there was a small room where I was before, and that is where we spent two days and then the International Red Cross was to come and then they took us altogether and took us away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when you were taken back into the white house you were not taken to the small room at the end of the corridor, to the toilet area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you were taken away from Omarska when the International Red Cross was to come, where were you taken from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje, not from Omarska, to the hangar, from the white house to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you left Omarska camp, when you were taken from Omarska camp, you were taken to Trnopolje camp, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until August 21st.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Trnopolje camp, did you know any of the guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those guards that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew Mladen Baltic, Djurdjevic, then Mladen Karajica, Baltic, Cavic -- I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you knew someone called Karajica. Had you known of a family known Karajica prior to your being taken to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the names of the Karajica men that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Sveto Karajica, Sreto's father, Mladen was son. Well, there were quite a number of them. I do not know the names of each one of them, but I know them. I cannot remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you know a Sveto Karajica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eldest, the oldest among them. He was older than I am.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was his name Sveto or Sreto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sreto is his son, Sreto is Sveto's son. Sreto is Mladen's father. Mladen is quite young, like my son.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many sons did Sveto have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two, Sreto and another one. I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sreto had how many sons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had two sons, Mladen and another one. I have forgotten his name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you also knew guards at Trnopolje whose name was Cavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know the first name of any of those guards named Cavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, there were three or four Cavics, this one, the shortest one, he be the worst.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The shortest one. Do you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The side of Trnopolje, towards Petrov Gaj, perhaps about a kilometre from the camp at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know with whom he lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His mother.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where his mother worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the paper and pulp factory in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Cavics who worked at the camp, did they live in the Trnopolje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you left Trnopolje on 21st August. Did you become part of a large convoy that ultimately went to Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At some point on Vlasic Mountain, were the men in the buses that were part of your group told to get off those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we came near Vlasic, up to Vlasic, there were three bus fulls of men and they were all unloaded there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you also told to take all of your personal belongings with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told us we did not need any things and that they could stay on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you were taken off the bus with these other men, did you manage to get on a truck that was part of the large convoy and so continue with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then you ultimately arrived in Bosnian government territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the attacks in opstina Prijedor, were you a member of any anti-Serb military or paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I was not a member of any organisation, never. I have never been a member of any organisation. I did not meddle in politics. I simply did my job.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What permanent injuries or medical problems do you have as a result of the beatings and treatment that you received in the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have frequent headaches and nightmares. I have kidney complaints. My arm hurts when I try to raise it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you have testified that you had both your upper and lower teeth knocked out at the camps. Have you now had those teeth replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier identified Dule Tadic in this courtroom. The man that you identified in the courtroom, is that the man who beat you in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is that the man who beat you and your son in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. We have been communicating in an effort to resolve some of the technical problems that we are trying to provide, with the technical facilities I should say, that we are trying to provide for the parties in order to continue to receive testimony. So, that is the reason for the delay. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis you had concluded direct had you?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I had your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Elezovic, you told us that while you were at Keraterm you were interviewed by a man called Radakovic. Did you know him before that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not hear? I did not understand the question well. Did I know Rade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Radakovic, the man you said who interviewed you at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know him before that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. I did not associate with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you knew his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him as a director of the National Park.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you learn his name as being Radakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found it out from the prisoners who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, his name has been told to you by someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You describe the man who was with him as being Dule Tadic. You said he was his bodyguard. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he was with him. He did not beat me, only Dule beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you told the name of that man by other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Dule Tadic from sight, but I heard that he wrote threat letters to himself. Apparently, Muslims were writing it against him but, apparently, there were controls so people knew it was him who wrote letters on his own behalf and that is the man. That is how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know the name of Dusko Tadic after the interview, that he had been there with Radakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You do not seem to have known Dusko Tadic very well, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not associate with him, but I knew of him, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned something about threatening letters that had been in the newspaper, and that ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that it was in the papers. I heard from people that they were threatening him, but he was, apparently, that they were all good people, and so it turned out that he wrote his own letters but I did not know. I asked who he was and they said, "This is the man".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That must have been at a time quite near to the attack on Kozarac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in '91 or '92 which is before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it comes to this, that in 1991 until this matter of the threatening letters you did not know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his face but I did not know his name. It was of no interest to me at that time, like many other people that I did not have any contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But after the threatening letters you say that you learnt his name from other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that name Dule, Dule, but I did not know who he was until people pointed him to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems from what you tell us then that you had not spent any time with Dule Tadic, you and he had not been in the same company together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never was in company with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you are in Omarska, you see again Radakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Radakovic did not interview you in Omarska. He just happened to be in the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- interrogation centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a first room as you come up the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you came across this man in the two places, Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After you had been interviewed, you then went to the white house but were taken around the back of the white house where you have told us that you were badly beaten by Dusko Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Keraterm, it was Dusko who beat me, not in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Omarska were you telling us that Dusko Tadic beat you after you had been interviewed the second time and you were taken around the back of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken there from the interrogation which was upstairs where the kitchen was and then behind the white house, and there was a group of people that were beating and Dule Tadic with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of any other people who were in that group who were beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know or recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The faces, sort of, but not the names. They were mostly people from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The number of people who were being beaten when you were taken to the back of the white house, how many people were receiving these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 50, 60 people, a lot of people. There were dead people, alive, there were people groaning, showing signs of life. They were not shooting. They were just beating them with sticks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is what I want to ask you about. This does not seem to have been a place where knives or guns were being used to kill people, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just some hard objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Out of the people who seem to have survived this, it comes down to you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks as if, from what had been planned behind the white house, I passed out and that saved me. I have a knife stab wound on my leg and I did not even notice when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But of those people who were there receiving this beating, only you survived, is that what you understand to be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At some stage you notice one of the prisoners who has no shoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was when I came to later when they were loading the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was another prisoner called Hodzic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But from what you had told us before, it was intended that you would be killed, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because instead of being at Keraterm, here you were in Omarska when this is taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say that you regained consciousness, it was only two prisoners who were left there, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were more. They had not picked them all up. They were loading them up at that time. I think that there were about four prisoners who were loading them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is, in fact, what I was asking you about, the number of prisoners who were alive who were moving the bodies. That was four of them, but there were no more guards or soldiers or anyone else around who had been doing the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a driver there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say "a driver", that is the driver who is in the truck who is to move the bodies, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You then move back to the white house where you are put in one of the rooms, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you walk there? How did you get into the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That Hodzic helped me and another, one Bahti. I think he was an Albanian. He was driving the bread truck around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you are in that room, did Hodzic have your son's shoes on at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I started towards the white house, he had them on. He put them on when he was loading the bodies. I -- Bahti said, "Lie down" and then he said, "We will take you back when we are done".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But of all the other bodies that were there that you have told us about, there were other pairs of shoes, presumably, on those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why he took it from my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it seems a coincidence that it is you and they are your son's shoes that he has got on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe that is also because they were cousins, maybe as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So Hodzic is a cousin of your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So Hodzic would also be related to you, a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would be my relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems from all this that happened, of the people doing the beatings, all you can identify by name is Dusko Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The only person to survive as a witness was you, is that right? You see, have you been told a story by someone else, Mr. Elezovic, about what happened behind that white house and come to tell this court as if it was your own experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean that I am making it up, this story?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that you were not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived through all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you said Zigic had been to room 3 in Keraterm and there was machine gunning of people in that room, you did not know that Zigic had been there, did you because you did not see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him, but people who knew him said that he was the worst there and then the two twin brothers, Banovic. I was there but I did not see what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, and you did not see Zigic taking part in that, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am suggesting to you, you see, is this, that someone has told you that Dule was there on an occasion when your son was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule also beat me there together with my son, with a group of people. He was not alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you tell us, it was intended that you would be killed, that you were in the right place now to be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you left the white house, you were put in another part of Omarska camp, another room, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that room in the larger building we see on the model in the middle of the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember whereabouts in the building you were then at the end of your stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you go up the stairs, I think it is the second door to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that have been called room 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how it was called, maybe it was, but it was the second room and across from it, it was something like a Red Cross. There was the person without an arm who worked there. He was from Petrov Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is one other matter I need to question you about and it is this. Is it correct that you have seen programmes on television about Omarska camp and the arrest of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have not spoken to Monika Gras yourself, given television interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I do not know who I spoke to -- I did give a statement, a statement in Goettingen -- I think it was Kellerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you given interviews to newspapers, to The Times of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be, on several occasions I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you been interviewed for television programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for ZDF once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you seen on television programmes about Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not watch the Monika Gras film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Elezovic, you indicated that you had known Dule Tadic by sight in Kozarac, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that then there was an incident involving some letters, and after that incident did someone you knew point Dule Tadic out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So at that point in time you linked the face with which you were familiar with the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This face was the face of a person you had seen on occasions prior to that in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is the person in this courtroom today, the accused you pointed out earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Elezovic, when you told this court the story about you being taken behind the white house, seeing your son being beaten, you being beaten and then awakening to find your dead son beside you, were you lying to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you telling them the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was telling the truth. Unfortunately, it is truth.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you said when you were in Keraterm the accused that you pointed out beat you, were you lying to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not lie, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw that man in Keraterm, did you recognise him as Dule Tadic from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw that man in Omarska beating you and your son, did you recognise him as Dule Tadic from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I knew that I was finished.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have a few questions, Mr. Elezovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You testified that the population in Trnopolje was mixed, both Serbs and Muslims, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. There were other nations. There were Croats, Ukrainians, Poles. There were different nations in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of the population in Trnopolje was Serb and what percentage was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was more Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You testified that the Trnopolje residents were told to turn in their weapons. Were Serbs as well as Muslims told to turn in their weapons, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when Serbs were the ones who were arming themselves, only the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You also testified that the cleansing began on July 9th, 1992, and that were you helping Serb neighbours in their field when the soldiers came to take you. What were the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that day.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: --- nature of the relations between Serbs and Muslims in Trnopolje at that time? Did they get along? Were there tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were tensions, but we saw what was coming.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you see what was coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started shelling, when they attacked Kozarac, when they cleansed part of Kozarac, they left us until the end, more than a month. To live normally -- it was not normal, you could not go anywhere. What supplies of food you had, that is what you had to eat, you had to help them, you had to work and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there any shelling of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a few shells around the mosque fell. I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did that start, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May, 23rd, 24th. I do not know the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Before the shelling in Kozarac, what were the relations like between Serbs and Muslims? Did you get along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody got along well. Before the conflict the life was good, everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will we hear, Miss Hollis -- if my memory is correct, at least I have not heard a lot about Trnopolje -- more about what happened in Trnopolje? We have heard a lot about what led up to the conflict in Kozarac and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So I can stop asking questions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, you can ask as many as you like. We hope to have more information.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Do you have additional questions in the light of my questions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Elezovic, prior to 9th July when Elezovici and that particular area were cleansed, to your knowledge had other villages, other hamlets, near you such as Sivci been cleansed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened before us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Elezovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elezovic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, do you need any redaction -- no.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Given the current circumstances of the witness, no, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very good. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the Prosecution calls Said Grozdanic. Mr. Said Grozdanic, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Said Grozdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd January '67.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornji Garevci Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you raised in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live there up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far is Gornji Garevci from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven kilometres and two kilometres north of the road to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you arrested after the attack in the Kozarac area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25th May, '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were arrested where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were taken to Keraterm by bus, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were at the camp in Omarska were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you beaten at any stage when you were at this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to being taken to the Omarska camp, were you a member of any military or paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin or nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While at Omarska camp, for how long did you stay at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 27th May until 21st August, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 6th August 1992 were a large number of the prisoners called out of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to these prisoners that were called out on that day, on 6th August '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were called out I did not know where they were then, but I heard from guards that some had gone to Manjaca and others to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this day did a large number of the prisoners that had been kept at Omarska, were they bussed off to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners were left in the camp after these people left in the buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you included in that group of 180 remaining prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the majority of the prisoners had left the Omarska camp, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing we had to do was to clean up the camp. Secondly, during the night beds had arrived, so we made beds. That is what happened the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These beds, they arrived from outside of the camp, did they, by a truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They must have. There was some kind of a truck. I did not see where it had come from, but I saw the truck full of beds and it was there while we were taking the beds in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you make up the beds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the building together with the kitchen which was in Omarska. It was from the east as you enter that building. I remember that. There were some offices there. There was a garage there, but that was the second door, the first door of the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told why you had to make up these beds after the other prisoners had left? Did anyone tell you why you were doing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you later find out why you were making up these beds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not learn it but we could guess why, so that it would look better for the journalists when they came, so as to disguise what had happened in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you been told that journalists were coming to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you permitted to sleep in these beds once you had made them up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the first time, we were not allowed. Sometimes it was allowed, sometimes it was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything happen with the supply of food and rations to you after the majority of the prisoners had gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They began to give us then two times a day, and then we did not have to run for food any more because they ordered us, when we were going for meals, to walk slowly, so that when the journalists came that we had to, that we were to say that we had been in the camp for two or three weeks and ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. Were you told by the guards at the camp what you were to say to the journalists about the camp, what sort of a camp it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you told to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the journalists would come they told us to mind what we were saying, what we would say, because we were still in their hands, so that, how shall I put it, so that they could still do with us whatever they liked or ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was it who told you this, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic came many times. I did not know his name but I learnt it after the long time that I spent in Omarska. He used to say that we had been here for two or three weeks and that we had to eat twice a day, that nobody had laid a finger on us until then and that we would be released within seven days, that we were there only for interrogation purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These things you were told to tell the journalists if asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the making up of the beds, were the prisoners that were retained behind in Omarska required to do other things in terms of cleaning up the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we cleaned the white house, the hangar, moved the flower tubs, those concrete pots, well, whatever, just to disguise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say about the concrete pots, where were these concrete pots located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were between the hangar and the kitchen on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were the pots moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that we moved them, but why and how did we move them, I do not remember because it did not matter then why should I move it. I only know that we had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that you had to clean up the white house. What did you discover when you went into the white house that had to be cleaned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not I, I did not go to clean the white house. I saw others go to clean it, but these buildings are about 50 metres one from the other. I did not go there, the others did. What did they clean there? I did not ask them what they did there. All I saw was go in to clean it, but why ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you there in Omarska camp when the journalists arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you discover where these journalists had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know whether they were Serbian or from Yugoslavia, from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once one could see that they came, they spoke in a language I could understand, and they all spoke like that. So, presumably, they were not foreign journalists because they all spoke our language. Then one was shooting, recording, how you had to say that everything is all right. When foreign journalists came they would have an interpreter and you knew they were foreign. On a couple of occasions they came when they spoke the language that I understand Serbo-Croatian and they talked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you say that some of the journalists that came spoke your language and others used interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some did not need interpreters, because when he comes he asks you when an interpreter comes, then you hear because when the journalist who asks questions he speaks a foreign language and the interpreter asks you what he asks you, and then you reply. When one who speaks my language comes, then presumably he is not a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. On 21st August 1992 did you then leave Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Manjaca for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until December 14th. I cannot remember the date. I know it was December, but was it 14th or the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So about mid-December. Did you then leave Manjaca camp and did you go to Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Grozdanic being permanently excused, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have five minutes remaining until the time that we typically adjourn, and we thought we would not hear from another witness but address two other matters. The first has to do with the request of the Defence to have a short recess after the Prosecutor concludes its case in-chief. I believe you had requested a week or two weeks, Mr. Wladimiroff, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have considered that and that -- what is the position of the Prosecutor? I do not know that you had a position, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no position on it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That request will be granted. So when the Prosecutor concludes its case in-chief we will then recess for two weeks in order for the Defence to use that time. The other matter related to, this had to do with the request of the Prosecutor to interview alibi witnesses during that recess. As I recall, the Defence did not oppose that and the Defence and the Prosecutor had met, discussed this matter and it had been agreed that the Prosecutor could interview those witnesses with the Defence counsel present, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We set up the conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, we have discussed the matter and it was clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The motion then of the Prosecutor that is outstanding regarding supplementing the response to the alibi notice, will be granted in so far as you need not respond until after you have spoken with the alibi witnesses. How much time do you think you will need thereafter, Mr. Niemann, to file the notice regarding any rebuttal witnesses? If you wish, you may confer and advise us tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Judge Stephen was suggesting that I ask you whether you have a better estimate of when you would conclude your evidence-in-chief. I added up the numbers just a few minutes ago and I have come to 47 hours, if I accept the time that you have listed. How does that sound?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You need whatever time is listed on your witness list, or will you be not calling some of those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are a couple of witnesses we may not call, your Honour, but our estimate at the moment I think is still around about the second or the third week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You might take a look at your witness list and perhaps tomorrow morning you can give us an estimate of how much time is needed. We are not suggesting that you in any way curtail your evidence, but we were just wondering what was your estimate as we stand now. Very good. Are there any additional matters we could use the two minutes for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is one additional matter, your Honours. I am not sure whether or not it is going to affect these proceedings in any way, but I think it is appropriate that I should raise the fact that it is suggested that there may be difficulties operating in Bosnia during the period of the election from 1st to 21st September. I just raise that at this point because at least the Office of the Prosecutor has been put on notice that all resources in Bosnia will be utilized for that purpose at that time, and they are not in a position to accommodate any of our requirements. I know this is a Defence matter but I raise it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting you may have some difficulty interviewing then the Defence witnesses? If we do recess the end of August or the first week in September for one to two weeks, are you saying that you may not be able to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have certainly been put on notice in terms of our other activities in Bosnia, that during that period the resources of IFOR and other agencies are so fully committed with the election lead-up to it that they will not be able to accommodate any of our requirements. Whether that impacts upon these proceedings or whether it impacts upon the Defence I am not able to say, but I raise it because it is a matter which has been drawn to our attention.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Those are matters over which we have absolutely no control. I imagine we will look at the newspapers along with you, but let us see what develops as we move into the month of August and perhaps we will have a better read as to it. We will adjourn then until tomorrow at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.).

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
(The court adjourned until the following day)
